title: A project with version history
summary: Save two meaningful commits and restore a deliberately broken change.
explanation: Git records versions you choose to save. A commit is a saved snapshot with a message explaining the change. Your working files can contain edits that are not committed. Staging selects the changes for the next commit; committing records that selection. Git does not automatically save every edit, and a local commit does not publish anything.

Use a disposable new folder called history-demo. Put a main.js file there that prints Hello. From its parent, this terminal sequence creates local history. Git must be installed, and the example identity is only for this disposable repository:
```bash
cd history-demo
git init
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
git status
git add main.js
git commit -m "Add greeting"
```
init creates a repository; local config supplies an author identity; status shows file state. add stages main.js, and commit records that staged version with the supplied message.

Now edit main.js in your editor so it prints Hello, reader and save it. Run it to confirm the greeting, then use:
```bash
git diff
git add main.js
git commit -m "Improve greeting"
git log --oneline -2
```
diff shows unstaged changes. The second commit saves the improvement. log --oneline -2 shows the newest two commits as short identifiers and messages. Staging is a step before the commit; it does not delete old history.

For recovery practice, deliberately change that greeting to broken in this disposable file and save it. First inspect the difference and copy any uncommitted work you want to keep outside the file. Then run:
```bash
git status
git diff
git restore --source=HEAD -- main.js
node main.js
```
HEAD means the current commit. restore replaces this uncommitted file with HEAD's version; -- separates the file path from options. The program prints Hello, reader again. This discards the selected file's uncommitted change, so preserve wanted edits before restoring.

A committed mistake needs a different recovery. git revert with the mistake's commit id creates a new commit reversing it, preserving history. For example, in a disposable repository where the newest commit is the mistake, git revert HEAD reverses that commit and records the reversal. Review the chosen commit first; an older change can conflict with later work. Avoid destructive reset commands while learning this workflow.

For the exercise, restore returns a copy of the last versions entry. The supplied history has two entries, so the latest code is Hello, coder and the original first entry remains Hello. The function assumes a nonempty history, as supplied. Finish the local Git task as well: inspect two meaningful commits, recover one uncommitted mistake, and rerun the restored program. The browser model cannot establish that real Git history exists on your computer.

title: A reproducible project
summary: Declare dependencies and write instructions for running the project.
explanation: A reproducible project can be started from a clean copy using written instructions. A dependency is a package the code uses. package.json describes the project, needed packages, and runnable scripts. A lockfile, usually package-lock.json for npm, records the exact resolved package versions. Those are different jobs: a version range allows choices; the lockfile records the choices actually made.

Create main.js in the same disposable repro-demo folder with console.log('Clean start works');. Use these commands from the folder:
```bash
node --version
npm install
npm start
npm ci
npm start
```
The version check reports your runtime. install reads the manifest and creates or updates the lockfile when needed. start prints Clean start works. Once a matching lockfile exists, ci performs a clean installation using its recorded dependency versions, then the second start should work too. ci replaces node_modules, so use a clean practice copy for this walkthrough.

npm install and npm ci are not interchangeable in every situation. ci needs an existing lockfile that agrees with package.json; it fails instead of silently changing an inconsistent lockfile. Keep the manifest and lockfile in project history. node_modules contains installed package files and can usually be recreated. A lockfile improves consistency but does not promise identical behavior across every operating system or runtime version.

A README should tell another person the runtime requirement, setup command, launch command, and expected behavior. Here is plain example content, not a program:
```text
Repro demo
Requires Node.js 22.13 or newer.
Initial setup: npm install
Keep the generated package-lock.json.
Clean-copy setup with that lockfile: npm ci
Launch: npm start
Expected output: Clean start works
Third-party runtime dependencies: none
```
Test these instructions on a fresh copy so missing steps become visible. A screenshot of a successful run cannot replace the saved dependency information.

After the declaration passes, download the supplied files and follow the README locally. Confirm both the initial install and a clean-copy install with its saved lockfile, then start the program. title: A reviewed AI change
summary: Describe a small feature, review an AI proposal, apply it, and check the result.
explanation: An AI coding proposal is a proposed change you need to understand and verify. Describe the promised behavior with examples before reviewing it: who should get a discount, how much, and what happens for invalid input. A confident explanation is not proof that code satisfies those requirements. Read the changed lines, then check the behavior that matters.

Validation should happen before the calculation. Number.isFinite checks that price is an actual finite number; it rejects NaN, Infinity, and numeric text. price < 0 rejects a negative number, while 0 is valid. Membership must be the boolean true, not merely a truthy value. Nonempty strings such as 'false' are truthy in JavaScript, so if(isMember) alone can accidentally grant them a discount.

For the exercise, the discount is ten percent rather than this walkthrough's twenty percent. Ten percent of 80 is 8, so a member keeps 80 - 8 = 72, equivalent to 80 × 0.9. A nonmember keeps 80. Validate the price first, then choose the member calculation. isMember === true prevents a string from receiving the discount. Invalid negative, NaN, or Infinity prices return null.

Review meaningful cases: valid member, valid nonmember, zero, negative, non-finite value, and a truthy string posing as membership. Keep the earlier working code in History or Git so you can recover if the proposal breaks a promised behavior. Explain why each branch exists before accepting it. For real money, fractional representation and rounding rules also need explicit decisions; this small number exercise checks the supplied arithmetic rule.

Implement finalPrice with the supplied names and confirm all relevant checks. An AI that changes only the first example might still get the nonmember case wrong. Ask for a focused explanation or hint when a line is unclear, then inspect and test it yourself. If a new change causes a regression, restore the known working version while investigating instead of treating the AI's reassurance as evidence.

analogy.familiar: Checking someone else’s homework steps
analogy.connection: A useful suggestion still needs you to follow the steps and check the result.
analogy.limit: The assistant can make mistakes even when the explanation sounds confident.

steps: Write finalPrice(price,isMember). Return null if price is negative, is not a number, or is NaN or Infinity.
Apply a ten-percent discount only when isMember is true; otherwise return the original price.
Test price 100 with and without membership, zero, -1, NaN, and Infinity.
If the tutor is connected, ask it to review your change.
Explain each condition in your own words.
Practice recovery by restoring an earlier saved version.
starter:
function finalPrice(price,isMember){return price*0.9;}
console.log(finalPrice(100,false));
solution:
function finalPrice(price,isMember){if(!Number.isFinite(price)||price<0)return null;return isMember===true?price*0.9:price;}
console.log(finalPrice(100,false));

checks.label: Members get the discount; other shoppers do not
Empty-price boundary and invalid cases are safe
Only Boolean true receives the discount

quiz.question: An AI change passes one example. What should you do next?
choices: Accept every later change automatically
Review the changed code and check relevant edge cases
Hide errors from the output
quiz.explanation: One example is limited evidence. Review what changed and test the behaviors the feature promises.

hints: A valid price must be finite and at least zero.
Check invalid input before applying any discount.
Use isMember to choose between price * 0.9 and price.

math.explanation: The discount needs two valid conditions: a valid price and membership. Missing membership keeps the original valid price.
math.question: For price 80 and membership false, what is the final price?

title: A tested feature
summary: Check normal, empty, boundary, failure, and concurrency cases where applicable.
explanation: A useful test checks promised behavior by comparing actual and expected results. It should fail when that behavior breaks. For clamping, a valid number below the range becomes the lower limit, one above becomes the upper limit, and one already inside stays unchanged. First reject the wrong kind of input; then apply the boundaries.

Run the test locally with Node installed:
```bash
node --test test-level.mjs
```
Passing assertions produce a passing test report. The module's demonstration console logs may also appear because importing evaluates that module. Temporarily replace the clamp with return value and rerun: outside-range assertions should fail. Restore the working code afterward. A test that only confirms the function exists would not catch that broken behavior.

Choose cases from the feature's requirements. Normal input verifies ordinary use; boundaries verify the exact included endpoints; just-outside values verify the transition; invalid input verifies rejection. Empty input can mean undefined here rather than a zero-length list. Concurrency tests are useful for shared balance updates, but this pure calculation has no shared mutable state, so concurrency is not a relevant risk for it.

For clampScore, use the exercise's 0-through-100 limits and preserve null for non-integers. Check 42, 0, 100, -5, and 110, plus undefined, NaN, Infinity, and 2.5. The inside result 100 and the just-outside result for 101 are both 100, but for different reasons: the first is already valid; the second must be clamped. Together they test the boundary transition.

The browser checks your function's behavior. Download score.mjs and test.mjs, replace the supplied score stub with your implementation, and run node --test test.mjs from their folder. A working browser function does not automatically edit that local stub. Break a relevant behavior briefly and confirm the local test fails, then restore and rerun. Passing tests are evidence for their stated cases, not proof of every possible property.

analogy.familiar: Trying a door from both sides and checking its latch
analogy.connection: Several meaningful checks tell you more than looking at the door once.
analogy.limit: More tests do not guarantee correctness if all tests miss the same important behavior.

steps: Write clampScore. Return null unless the input is a number with no decimal part. Negative integers are allowed; NaN and Infinity are not.
Return 0 for numbers below 0 and 100 for numbers above 100. Keep numbers from 0 through 100 unchanged.
Add cases for 42, 0, 100, -5, 110, undefined, NaN, Infinity, and 2.5.
Download score.mjs and test.mjs. Put your clampScore function in score.mjs.
From their folder, run node --test test.mjs.
Temporarily make the function wrong and check that a test catches the mistake.
Restore the working function and run the tests again.
starter:
function clampScore(value){return value;}
console.log(clampScore(110));
solution:
function clampScore(value){if(!Number.isInteger(value))return null;return Math.max(0,Math.min(100,value));}
console.log(clampScore(110));

checks.label: Outside values clamp to the nearest limit

quiz.question: clampScore should reduce integer scores above 100 to 100. A broken version returns those scores unchanged. Which assertion would expose that bug?
choices: clampScore(60) === 60
clampScore(100) === 100
clampScore(125) === 100
quiz.explanation: 125 exercises the above-maximum path: the correct result is 100, but the broken version returns 125. The other assertions use already-allowed values and can still pass despite this bug.

hints: Reject non-integers first. Number.isInteger also rejects NaN and Infinity.
Math.min(100, value) applies the upper limit.
Wrap the result in Math.max(0, ...) for the lower limit.

math.explanation: A correctness claim needs its assumptions. Here the input must be an integer, and the output must fall inside the allowed range.
math.question: Why test both 100 and 101?
choices: To check the included boundary and the value immediately outside it
Because they should always return different outputs
Because zero is never a boundary
math.feedback: 100 is already valid; 101 must be reduced to 100. Together they check the transition at the upper limit.

title: A maintainable published app
summary: Deploy a small app, check its health, and reproduce a failure using useful logs.
explanation: Deployment makes a particular built version available to its intended users. Record a release identifier so you can tell which version is served and which previous version to restore. A successful local run proves only the local run. After deployment, check a response from the actual published app for the expected version and behavior.

A macOS terminal can start that disposable local server with a deliberate storage failure:
```bash
RELEASE_ID=demo-4 STORAGE_READY=false node health-server.mjs
```
While it runs, use another terminal:
```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3030/health
```
-i includes response headers. Expect 503 and version demo-4. Stop the server with Control-C, restart with STORAGE_READY=true, and request again; expect 200. This flag simulates readiness, so it does not actually probe a database or prove all screens work.

Logs are recorded events that help investigate problems. A useful failure record might contain requestId, releaseId, and a category such as storage-unavailable. Match an observed failure to its log using the request id. Avoid logging passwords, keys, or private message content. Reproduce a failure in a disposable local test before guessing at a fix. Observability means having enough useful evidence to understand what the running app is doing.

Before release, run relevant checks, confirm the intended audience, and identify the previous working version. Record that evidence and your hosting provider's restore procedure in RELEASE.md. Rollback returns the served app to that working version; saved-data changes may need separate backup or migration recovery. Practice restoration in a private test environment and check its actual version afterward.

For the exercise, health(appReady, storageReady, version) returns numeric 200 only when both conditions are ready, otherwise 503, and includes version either way. The browser checks this decision function; Run performs no deployment. The supplied local server demonstrates a readiness flag and version, not every dependency. Actual hosting, health verification, and rollback are separate tasks in your chosen private provider project and may involve account or usage costs. Follow that provider's instructions and verify the real served release.

analogy.familiar: Checking a delivered assignment against the saved final version
analogy.connection: The delivered version should match the one you checked, and you should know how to recover the earlier copy.
analogy.limit: A health check is limited evidence; it does not test every screen or behavior.

steps: Write health(appReady,storageReady,version). The app is ready only when both appReady and storageReady are true.
Return {status:200,version} when ready, otherwise {status:503,version}.
Build a small local server using the supplied file, then follow your hosting provider’s private-deployment instructions.
Check the published app’s /health response.
In a separate local test, start the supplied server with STORAGE_READY set to false.
Write a log entry that includes the requestId and the reason for the failure.
In RELEASE.md, record the release ID and your hosting provider’s steps for restoring the previous version.
Practice restoring the previous version in a private test environment.
starter:
function health(appReady,storageReady,version){return {status:200,version};}
console.log(health(true,false,'lesson-1'));
solution:
function health(appReady,storageReady,version){return {status:appReady&&storageReady?200:503,version};}
console.log(health(true,false,'lesson-1'));

quiz.question: How can you check that users are getting the new release?
choices: Only a local build message
A response from the published app showing the expected release ID
An old screenshot
quiz.explanation: Check the actual served version and its expected behavior after deployment.

hints: Readiness combines the app and storage with AND.
Use appReady && storageReady to choose 200 or 503.
Keep version in both the success and failure result.

extraFiles.name: server.mjs
extraFiles.code: import {createServer} from 'node:http';const version=process.env.RELEASE_ID||'lesson-1';createServer((req,res)=>{const ready=process.env.STORAGE_READY!=='false';res.writeHead(ready?200:503,{'Content-Type':'application/json'});res.end(JSON.stringify({status:ready?'ready':'not-ready',version}));}).listen(3000,'127.0.0.1');

extraFiles.code:
# Release practice

Release ID: fill in after building. Intended audience: private. Checks: record relevant checks. Deployed /health result: record after publishing. Previous version: record ID. Rollback: use the hosting provider’s documented version restore; test it privately. Do not include secrets in this note.

externalNotes: The app checks your health decision. Actual hosting and rollback use your chosen provider and can involve account or usage costs; complete them in a private test project. No deployment is performed by this lesson’s Run button.

title: A reviewed release
summary: Review permissions, secrets, input handling, dependency risks, and keyboard access.
explanation: A release review compares requirements with actual evidence. Check record permissions, secret handling, input validation, safe output, dependencies, and keyboard access. A checked box without a real observation proves little. Record findings, fixes, and remaining limits so someone reading the review can understand what was verified.

Displaying untrusted text safely matters. This complete browser HTML example uses textContent: ```html Safe text demo

``` The paragraph shows the literal characters Hello. textContent treats the string as text. innerHTML would interpret the tags as markup. eval would interpret suitable text as JavaScript. Use a reviewed sanitizer when a feature truly requires supplied HTML.

Server validation checks input shape, size, and allowed ranges before a write. Permission tests should use two users and attempt access to another user's records. Keep secrets outside browser code, repository history, and logs: anything shipped to the browser can be read by its user. Dependency review compares declared packages and shipped versions with current advisories; a past clean report may be stale.

Accessibility review checks whether people can identify and use controls. Inputs need meaningful labels, keyboard focus should be visible, Tab order should follow the task, and errors should explain what to fix. This complete HTML example supplies a label and native keyboard-accessible button:
```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Label demo</title></head>
<body>
  <form>
    <label for="minutes">Practice minutes</label>
    <input id="minutes" type="number" min="1" max="180" required>
    <button type="submit">Save practice</button>
  </form>
</body>
</html>
```
Tab reaches the field and then the button. The label's for matches the input id. Browser number bounds assist input but do not replace server validation. This page has no save server, so it demonstrates labeling and keyboard controls rather than persistence.

Three independent true/false requirements create 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. Only true/true/true passes, so there is one allowed combination. One missing or false requirement is enough to fail. A truthy string is not a completed review; strict comparison prevents 'true' from being treated as evidence. The function assumes it receives a review object; validating an entirely missing argument would be an additional input contract.

For canRelease, check permissionChecks, secretChecks, and keyboardChecks with === true, joined by &&. Then use the supplied REVIEW.md against a real private project: test account separation, inspect shipped code and logs for secrets, try invalid and oversized input, inspect dependencies, and complete the core task with keyboard alone. Include safe output, labels, errors, and recoverability. The browser verifies your decision function; it cannot establish the real project's security or accessibility review.

analogy.familiar: Checking an assignment against its stated requirements
analogy.connection: You compare each requirement with evidence before calling the work finished.
analogy.limit: A checked list is not evidence unless the actual behavior was tested.

steps: Write canRelease(review). Return true only when permissionChecks, secretChecks, and keyboardChecks are all the Boolean value true.
Do not accept missing values or the string "true" as a passed review.
Run cases where one requirement is false or missing.
Use the supplied checklist on a private project you are allowed to test.
Check that one test user cannot read or change another test user’s private records.
Inspect the JavaScript sent to the browser and check that it contains no secrets.
Try using the whole app with only the keyboard.
Before releasing, write down what you checked, what happened, what you fixed, and what still does not work.
starter:
function canRelease(review){return !!review.permissionChecks;}
console.log(canRelease({permissionChecks:true,secretChecks:false,keyboardChecks:true}));
solution:
function canRelease(review){return review.permissionChecks===true&&review.secretChecks===true&&review.keyboardChecks===true;}
console.log(canRelease({permissionChecks:true,secretChecks:false,keyboardChecks:true}));

checks.label: Missing or failed requirements stop release

quiz.question: An untrusted note contains "Hello". You must display those exact characters, not interpret HTML. Which change is safe for that display?
choices: Assign the note to textContent
Assign the note to innerHTML
Run the note through eval first
quiz.explanation: textContent inserts literal text. innerHTML interprets markup, and eval executes JavaScript rather than safely displaying the note.

hints: There are three mandatory conditions, joined by AND.
Compare every required value with true using ===.
Missing values and strings must produce false.

math.explanation: For three required true/false conditions, there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. Only the all-true combination allows release.
math.question: Release requires tests passed, review approved, and secrets absent. Tests and review pass, but a secret is present. Should release be allowed?
choices: Yes, two conditions passed
No, the secrets-absent condition failed
Yes, review overrides the other conditions
math.feedback: All three conditions are required. A present secret makes secrets absent false, so the AND condition blocks release even though the other two passed.

extraFiles.name: REVIEW.md
extraFiles.code:
# Private release review

For each item record evidence and unresolved limits.
- Account and record permissions: test two users.
- Secrets: inspect browser bundle, repository and logs.
- Input: normal, invalid, boundary, oversized values.
- Output: untrusted text is displayed safely.
- Dependencies: inspect declared packages and current advisories.
- Keyboard: every core action reachable; focus visible.
- Labels and errors: inputs and feedback understandable.
- Recoverability: test previous version and saved-data backup.

Release decision: record after actual checks.

externalNotes: The browser checks the release decision function. A real security and accessibility review requires the specific project and current dependency information; fill the checklist with actual evidence.

title: A tidy name badge
summary: Write badge(name): trim outside spaces and return "Hello, " plus the name. For an empty or spaces-only name, return "Hello, guest". Keep spaces inside the name.
explanation: A name typed into a form can contain extra spaces. A string is text. This project changes how that text is displayed without changing the original input. You already know functions and conditions; now you will combine them with a string method, an action attached to a text value.

Calling trim() removes whitespace from both ends of a string. Whitespace includes spaces and line breaks. The dot selects the method; parentheses call it. It does not squeeze spaces inside a name or change capital letters. Store the returned string, because JavaScript strings are not edited in place.

An empty string is written "". After trimming, compare the result with "" using ===. That comparison produces true or false. Decide on your fallback after cleanup, or a string containing only spaces could accidentally become a blank badge.

The plus sign joins strings here. Both "Hello, " and a cleaned name are strings. Keep the comma and one space in the greeting. This function accepts strings only; accepting numbers or objects would need a separate decision about validation. Do not silently change someone's name to a different capitalization.

Write badge(name) and keep it reusable: checks call it with different names, spaces and an empty string. Try a name containing two words. Predict which spaces should remain before running it. The checks examine returned values, so displaying a greeting with console.log alone does not complete the function.

analogy.familiar: A name card with empty space around the writing
analogy.connection: Cleanup removes unwanted space around the name before adding a greeting.
analogy.limit: This does not judge whether the name is valid or change its spelling.

steps: Create badge(name), which accepts a string.
Use trim() to remove spaces and other whitespace from the ends of the name. Then check whether anything is left.
Return "Hello, guest" if the cleaned name is empty. Otherwise, return "Hello, " followed by the cleaned name.
Run the checks and try a two-word name.

checks.label: Blank input gets a useful fallback
Inside spaces and letters are preserved
checks.expression: badge("  Ana  Lee  ") === "Hello, Ana  Lee" && badge("zoë") === "Hello, zoë"

quiz.question: What does "  Pine Grove  ".trim() return?
choices: "Pine Grove"
"PineGrove"
"  Pine Grove  "
quiz.explanation: trim removes outside whitespace and preserves the space between the two words.

hints: Keep the result of name.trim() in a variable.
Compare the cleaned string with "".
Join "Hello, " to either "guest" or the cleaned name.

title: A shared supply list
summary: Write totals(rows). Each row has item and quantity. Return a Map that adds quantities for identical item names. Keep first-seen item order and leave the input unchanged. Quantities are nonnegative integers.
explanation: Several people can request the same supply. A grouped total combines rows with the same item name. The input is an array of objects; each object has item and quantity. Your output will be a Map, a JavaScript collection that connects keys with values. An item name is the key and its running total is the value.

Create an empty Map with new Map(). Use set(key, value) to store a value and get(key) to read it. Getting a missing key returns undefined. Map keeps the order in which distinct keys were first inserted. Updating an existing key changes its value without moving it to the end.

The ?? operator chooses its right-hand value when its left-hand value is null or undefined. For a missing item, counts.get(item) ?? 0 gives you a starting total of zero. This also preserves an existing zero. A for...of loop can then visit every request exactly once.

Map treats ordinary strings such as "constructor" as ordinary keys. This avoids the special inherited properties found on a plain object. Names are compared exactly here: "Pen" and "pen" are separate items. The requirements do not ask you to clean names, so do not silently merge them.

Create a fresh Map inside totals each time. Read each row without changing it. An empty input should produce an empty Map, and a zero-quantity request should still create its item. The checks use repeated and unusual names as well as different totals; hard-coding the displayed sample will not satisfy them.

analogy.familiar: A supply sheet with one line per item
analogy.connection: Each Map key identifies the line whose total you update.
analogy.limit: Names are matched exactly; the Map does not know that two different spellings might mean the same item.

steps: Create a new Map inside totals.
For each row, look up the total already saved for that item. Use zero if the item has no saved total yet.
Add the row’s quantity to that total. Save the new total in the Map using the item name as its key.
Return the Map and try an empty list.

checks.label: Repeated supplies add in first-seen order
Empty, zero and unusual names work
Input stays unchanged and case stays distinct
checks.expression: (() => { const rows = Object.freeze([Object.freeze({item:"Pen",quantity:1}),Object.freeze({item:"pen",quantity:2})]); const result = totals(rows); return result.size === 2 && rows[0].quantity === 1; })()

quiz.question: After set("pen", 2) and set("pen", 7), how many entries use the key "pen"?
choices: Two entries
One entry, whose value is 7
One entry, whose value is 9
quiz.explanation: set replaces the value at an existing key. You must explicitly add the old quantity to get a total.

hints: Read row.item and row.quantity without changing the row.
Use result.get(row.item) ?? 0.
set the sum, then return result after the loop.

title: A task board that keeps its old copy
summary: Write toggleTask(tasks, id). Return a new array; copy the matching task with done reversed. Leave all other task objects and the original array unchanged. IDs are unique strings. If the ID is missing, return a new array with the same task objects.
explanation: A task board may need its old state for undo or comparison. Mutation means changing an existing value in place. An immutable update creates the changed parts as new values and keeps the old state intact. This project practices that pattern with an array of task objects.

An array contains references to objects. Copying the array with [...tasks] creates a new array, but its task objects are still shared. Changing copied[0].done would also affect the object seen through tasks[0]. To change one task safely, create a new object for that task too.

map calls a function for each array item and builds a new array from the returned values. Return a new object for the matching ID. Return the existing task for other IDs: unchanged objects can be shared safely because your function does not edit them. Preserve task order.

This is a shallow copy: nested objects would still be shared unless you copy the nested part you change. Our tasks contain an ID, a Boolean done value and optional other properties. Keep those properties with object spread. The function assumes unique IDs, so a single requested ID refers to at most one task.

Check four cases: an unfinished task becomes finished, a finished task becomes unfinished, a missing ID leaves values alone, and an empty list remains empty. All cases return a fresh array. Compare the original after each call: preserving its data is part of success, not just getting the new checkbox value right.

analogy.familiar: A revised task sheet while keeping the previous version
analogy.connection: The new array represents the revision and the copied task represents the change.
analogy.limit: Object spread is shallow, so nested data may still be shared.

steps: Use tasks.map() to make a new array without changing the original array.
When a task’s id matches, copy that task. In the copy, change done from false to true, or from true to false.
For other IDs, keep the original task objects without changing them.
Check that the original tasks stay unchanged and that the copied task keeps its title.

checks.label: The selected task toggles without losing its title
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[{id:"a",title:"Read",done:false}]; const n=toggleTask(t,"a"); return n!==t && n[0]!==t[0] && n[0].done===true && n[0].title==="Read" && t[0].done===false; })()

checks.label: Other tasks retain their identity and order
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[Object.freeze({id:"a",done:false}),Object.freeze({id:"b",done:true})]; const n=toggleTask(Object.freeze(t),"b"); return n[0]===t[0] && n[1].id==="b" && n[1].done===false; })()

checks.label: Missing IDs and empty lists return fresh arrays
checks.expression: (() => { const t=[{id:"a",done:false}]; const n=toggleTask(t,"missing"); const empty=[]; const e=toggleTask(empty,"a"); return n!==t && n[0]===t[0] && e!==empty && e.length===0; })()

quiz.question: Why is copying the array with `[...tasks]` not enough before changing a task object?
choices: It does not copy the array
Its task objects are still shared with the original
It changes every task immediately
quiz.explanation: The array is new, but its entries still refer to the original objects. Copy the object you will change as well.

hints: Use task.id === id to choose the task.
Write { ...task, done: !task.done } for the changed object.
Return the result of tasks.map, including when no ID matches.

title: A note editor with reversible history
summary: Write createHistory(initial), where notes are strings. Return methods current(), edit(text), undo(), redo(). Each method returns the current string. Undo/redo stop at the ends. Editing after undo discards the redo branch; editing the current text does nothing.
explanation: Undo needs more than the current note: it needs previous versions and a position within them. Model the editor with an array of strings and an index called a cursor. An invariant is a fact that must stay true: the cursor always points to an existing version, and current() returns that version.

A closure is a function that keeps access to variables from where it was created. createHistory can create versions and cursor, then return methods that share those variables. Each call to createHistory gets its own storage. The caller can operate the editor without directly changing its internal array.

Undo moves the cursor left if an earlier version exists. Redo moves it right if a later version exists. Neither action changes the array. At the first or last version, return the current text unchanged. Avoid negative indexes or reading past the final entry.

If the new text equals the current text, return immediately. A repeated edit should not create a duplicate undo step or remove a useful redo branch. Strings suit this exercise because callers cannot mutate a saved string in place. Saving arbitrary objects would require a clear copy or immutability policy.

Test sequences, not just isolated methods: edit A to B to C, undo to B, then edit D. Redo must remain D because C belongs to the abandoned branch. Also test an empty string, repeated undo at the beginning, duplicate edits and two independent histories. Those transitions expose mistakes a single happy path would miss.

analogy.familiar: A row of saved note cards with a marker on the current one
analogy.connection: Undo moves the marker; a new edit after undo replaces the cards ahead of it.
analogy.limit: Real editors may group keystrokes and limit history size; this exercise treats each edit call as one version.

steps: Inside createHistory, keep the saved versions and a cursor that points to the current version.
Return an object with current, edit, undo, and redo methods.
Do not let undo go before the first version or redo go past the last version.
If you undo and then make a new edit, remove the later versions from the old history.
Ignore an edit if its text is the same as the current text.
Create two histories and check that changing one does not change the other.

checks.label: Undo and redo stop at the history boundaries
checks.expression: (() => {const h=createHistory(""); return h.undo()==="" && h.edit("A")==="A" && h.edit("B")==="B" && h.undo()==="A" && h.undo()==="" && h.undo()==="" && h.redo()==="A" && h.redo()==="B" && h.redo()==="B";})()

checks.label: A new branch discards old redo steps
Duplicate edits preserve redo; histories are independent

quiz.question: Your saved note versions are Plan → Draft → Final. You undo to Draft, then edit it into Revised. What should redo return now?
choices: Final
Revised
Plan
quiz.explanation: The new edit discards the old future version Final. Revised is now the latest version, so redo stays there.

hints: Start with [initial] and cursor 0.
Keep versions.slice(0, cursor + 1) before adding a new version.
Check equality before trimming redo history.

title: A shelf label maker
summary: Write shelf_label(item, count). Return a string like "Pencil: 1 item" or "Pencil: 3 items". Count is a nonnegative integer. Use "item" only when count equals 1; return the item name unchanged.
explanation: A shelf label combines a name, a number and a unit. A string is text, while an integer is a whole number. Your function will format these values into one string. Formatting means choosing how values appear as text; it does not change the values stored in the input variables.

An f-string starts with f immediately before its opening quote. Braces { } mark expressions Python should evaluate and insert. A plain quoted string leaves braces as ordinary characters. Use a parameter name inside braces to make the result follow the input on every call.

This complete example inserts two values.
```python
name = "Tape"
rolls = 4
label = f"{name}: {rolls} rolls"
print(label)
```
It prints Tape: 4 rolls. Python converts the number to text within the f-string. The colon and spaces are literal characters that you chose for the label.

Choose the singular word when count == 1. The double equals sign compares values; a single equals sign assigns a value. Zero uses the plural form in this English label. The requirement accepts only nonnegative integer counts, so this exercise does not need to handle negative stock or fractions.

You can choose a word before formatting the final text.
```python
def ticket_label(count):
    word = "ticket" if count == 1 else "tickets"
    return f"{count} {word}"
print(ticket_label(1))
print(ticket_label(0))
```
The output is 1 ticket and 0 tickets. The conditional expression chooses one value. An ordinary if/else block would also work.

return gives the completed label to the caller. print displays something and returns None. Keep shelf_label useful for both screen display and later storage by returning the string. The caller can then decide whether to print it. Preserve punctuation and spaces as stated so labels have a consistent shape.

Test a count of zero, one and several items. Try a two-word name and a name with a non-English letter: the function should carry the name through unchanged. These examples check the boundary where the wording changes. A single sample with three items would not reveal a mistaken singular rule.

analogy.familiar: A printed label with spaces for a name and quantity
analogy.connection: The f-string fills those spaces using the current values.
analogy.limit: Formatting text does not change inventory or validate the count.

steps: Define `shelf_label(item, count)` with two inputs.
Use the word `"item"` only when `count == 1`.
Use the word `"items"` for every other count.
Return the label with an f-string, keeping the requested spaces and punctuation.
Try counts of zero, one, and twelve.
Try an item name with two words.
starter:
def shelf_label(item, count):
    # TODO: choose item/items and return the formatted label.
    return ""

print(shelf_label("Pencil", 3))
solution:
def shelf_label(item, count):
    word = "item" if count == 1 else "items"
    return f"{item}: {count} {word}"

print(shelf_label("Pencil", 3))

checks.label: Zero and larger counts use plural labels
Names are preserved exactly
checks.expression: shelf_label("Blue pen", 2) == "Blue pen: 2 items" and shelf_label("Café", 1) == "Café: 1 item"

quiz.question: The label-building function returns text but the caller never prints the returned value. What should you expect in a normal script?
choices: The returned label need not appear on screen
return always prints its text
The function must raise an error
quiz.explanation: Returning makes a value available to the caller. Printing is a separate effect; a script does not automatically display every return value.

title: An inventory import report
summary: Write read_stock(text). Parse CSV with headers item,quantity. Return {"totals": {...}, "rejected": n}. Trim item names; accept quantities containing only ASCII digits after trimming, including zero. Reject blank names and invalid or missing quantities. Add repeated valid items. Completely blank lines are ignored.
explanation: CSV means comma-separated values. It stores rows as text, often from a spreadsheet. A comma can also be part of a field, such as "Pens, blue", so splitting every line at every comma is unsafe. Python's standard csv module handles quoted fields and escaped quote characters for you.

csv.DictReader reads the first row as column names and returns dictionaries for following rows. io.StringIO lets a string behave like a text file, so the reader can process supplied text without writing a file. Import both csv and io. The input contract supplies the item and quantity headers and well-formed CSV quoting.

Here is a complete example with a comma inside a quoted name.
```python
import csv
import io
text = 'item,quantity\n"Pens, blue",2\nTape,1\n'
for row in csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(text)):
    print(row["item"], row["quantity"])
```
The first item is the single string Pens, blue. Quantities are still strings at this stage; the CSV reader does not choose numeric types for you.

Validation decides whether a row meets the project's requirements before you use it. Trim the item and quantity fields. A quantity must be nonempty and contain only characters from "0123456789". Reject -2, 2.5 and two. Leading zeroes such as 003 are accepted and represent 3. Missing fields can be None, so replace None with an empty string before trimming.

In (row.get("item") or ""), or returns the left value if it is true-like; otherwise it returns the right operand. None and empty text are false-like, so this expression supplies empty text before strip is called. It does not necessarily return a Boolean.

Validate first, then convert to an integer.
```python
raw = " 003 ".strip()
valid = bool(raw) and all(char in "0123456789" for char in raw)
if valid:
    amount = int(raw)
    print(amount)
```
It prints 3. The explicit character set matches this project's ASCII-digit contract; some broader Unicode digit tests accept characters that int cannot convert.

bool(raw) converts the supplied value to its truth value: bool("") is False, while bool("0") is True because the text is nonempty. This does not validate that text as an integer; the separate character checks do that.

Keep totals in a dictionary. totals.get(item, 0) reads the existing amount or starts at zero. Increase rejected for each invalid record and continue to the next record. csv.DictReader ignores completely blank lines; a row such as comma plus a quantity is a real record with a blank name and must be rejected.

dict.get takes a key and an optional default. It returns the stored value when that key exists, or the default when it does not; it does not insert the missing key.
```python
totals = {"Pens": 4}
print(totals.get("Pens", 0))
print(totals.get("Tape", 0))
print("Tape" in totals)
```
It prints 4, 0, and False. The dot selects get on totals; the comma separates the key from the fallback value.

Return both the totals and the rejection count so the caller can see what happened. This exercise rejects individual bad records; malformed CSV syntax and missing headers are outside its stated input contract. Test quoted commas, duplicate names, zero stock, a missing quantity and an empty file with only headers. Do not count the header as a stock row.

analogy.familiar: Checking a delivery sheet before adding items to a shelf
analogy.connection: Each valid row contributes stock; rejected rows are counted for review.
analogy.limit: The importer follows the written format and cannot decide whether a plausible number was typed incorrectly.

steps: Read the CSV rows with `csv.DictReader` and `io.StringIO`.
Remove extra spaces from the edges of each field.
Reject a row if its item name is blank.
Reject a quantity unless all its characters are digits from 0 to 9.
Convert valid quantities to `int`.
Add each quantity to the total for that item name.
Return `totals` and `rejected`.
Test a name that has a comma inside quotes.

checks.label: Quoted commas and duplicate names total correctly
Bad quantities, missing fields and blank names are rejected
Zero, padded digits and blank lines work

quiz.question: Why use csv.DictReader instead of splitting each row on commas?
choices: It automatically fixes every invalid quantity
Quoted fields can contain commas that are part of a value
It removes the need for headers
quiz.explanation: The CSV reader understands quoting, so a comma inside a quoted item name does not split that item into two columns.

hints: Use (row.get("quantity") or "").strip() for missing values.
Check raw is nonempty before all(char in "0123456789" for char in raw).
Increase totals[item] using totals.get(item, 0), and count invalid records separately.

title: A reading log summary
summary: Write reading_summary(text). The JSON input is a list of objects with book (string) and pages (nonnegative integer). Return {"books": distinct count, "pages": total, "by_book": totals dictionary}. Repeated book names combine; empty input list gives zero totals. Valid JSON and the stated field types are supplied.
explanation: JSON means JavaScript Object Notation, but many languages use it to exchange data. It stores strings, numbers, arrays, objects, true, false and null. Python's json module translates JSON text into Python values. Here, a JSON array becomes a list and each JSON object becomes a dictionary.

Use json.loads(text) to parse a string. The s in loads refers to a string; json.load instead reads from an open file. Parsing checks JSON syntax, but it does not prove the result has your intended fields. This exercise supplies valid records so you can focus on turning them into a useful summary.

This complete example reads two entries.
```python
import json
text = '[{"book":"River","pages":8},{"book":"River","pages":3}]'
entries = json.loads(text)
print(entries[0]["book"])
print(sum(entry["pages"] for entry in entries))
```
It prints River and 11. Index 0 selects the first list entry; the string key "book" selects a dictionary value.

A session is one record; a book may have several sessions. Counting records would overstate the number of distinct books. Group pages by the exact book name using a dictionary. Each new name creates one key, and later sessions add to that key. Capitalization is significant under this project's contract.

Here is a small grouped sum.
```python
by_book = {}
for entry in [{"book": "Hill", "pages": 4}, {"book": "Hill", "pages": 6}]:
    name = entry["book"]
    by_book[name] = by_book.get(name, 0) + entry["pages"]
print(len(by_book))
print(sum(by_book.values()))
```
It prints 1 and 10. len counts keys in the dictionary, while values() provides the grouped page totals.

A zero-page session still records a book name, so keep that name with a total of zero. The empty array [] has no names or pages; sum of an empty collection is zero. Return a dictionary with exactly the three requested result fields so callers can use it without reading printed text.

You can use json.dumps to turn a Python result back into JSON text when exporting, but this function must return the Python dictionary itself. Never use eval to parse outside data: it executes Python expressions. Test several sessions, several books and the empty list. Parsing malformed JSON or validating arbitrary field types is a separate extension.

analogy.familiar: Combining several reading sessions under each book title
analogy.connection: Each title gets one page total, even when it appears several times.
analogy.limit: Exact titles are the identifiers here; a real library may need unique IDs for books with the same title.

steps: Use `json.loads` to turn the JSON text into Python values.
Make a dictionary that adds up pages for each exact book name.
Count the dictionary keys to find the number of different books.
Add the dictionary values to find the total pages.
Return `books`, `pages`, and `by_book`.
Test an empty input list too.

checks.label: Repeated sessions combine while distinct books are counted
The empty list produces an empty summary
Zero sessions and exact book names are preserved

quiz.question: Three records all name the same book. How many different books are there?
choices: It depends on the page total
quiz.explanation: Sessions are separate records, but the same book name forms one dictionary key.

hints: A row is a dictionary; use entry["book"] and entry["pages"].
Use by_book.get(name, 0) before adding the next session.
len(by_book) counts distinct names; sum(by_book.values()) totals pages.

title: A workshop preparation planner
summary: Write plan(tasks), where a dictionary maps task names to lists of prerequisite names. Return each task once with all prerequisites before it. Visit task names and each prerequisite list in alphabetical order for a reproducible result. Return None if a prerequisite is missing or a cycle exists. Keep input unchanged; the empty dictionary returns [].
explanation: A workshop has tasks that depend on other tasks: paint requires sanding, and sanding requires cutting. A dependency is a task that must happen first. A graph describes these relationships using nodes for tasks and edges for dependencies. A valid ordering puts every prerequisite before the task that needs it.

A depth-first search follows prerequisites before finishing the current task. Recursion means a function calls itself on a smaller part of the problem. Keep a result list, a set of finished tasks and a set of tasks currently being visited. The visiting set describes the unfinished chain of calls, not every task you have ever seen.

This small example explores dependencies before printing a task.
```python
tasks = {"paint": ["sand"], "sand": []}
finished = set()
def visit(name):
    if name in finished:
        return
    for before in tasks[name]:
        visit(before)
    finished.add(name)
    print(name)
visit("paint")
```
It prints sand before paint. This first example assumes no cycles; your project must add cycle and missing-task handling.

A cycle means a chain comes back to an unfinished task, such as A needing B while B needs A. Neither can begin. Detect it by checking whether a task is already in visiting when you enter it. A finished task is different: it is safe to reuse and should not be added to the result twice.

The two sets have distinct jobs.
```python
visiting = {"build", "prepare"}
finished = {"collect"}
print("build" in visiting)
print("collect" in finished)
visiting.remove("prepare")
finished.add("prepare")
```
The two printed values are true. Moving a name from visiting to finished represents completing that task after its dependencies have been handled.

Before reading tasks[name], check that name exists. Return failure for missing prerequisites instead of inventing a task. Sort keys and dependency lists before visiting them to make the result reproducible. Sorting produces new lists, so it need not change the input. Independent tasks can have many valid orders; this project chooses one traversal rule for predictable checks.

Define the visit helper inside plan so each planning call gets its own result list and visiting and finished sets. A nested helper can read names from that enclosing call and mutate those lists and sets; adding to a set or appending to a list does not reassign the outer name. A return goes only to the immediate caller. Each caller must check whether its recursive visit failed and return failure too, so the outer plan can stop rather than return a partial ordering.

Return None when any visit fails; otherwise return the accumulated list. The result is called a topological ordering. Its dependency traversal visits nodes and edges once apart from sorting, but Python recursion has a depth limit, so very deep production graphs need an iterative version. Test a chain, shared prerequisites, a missing name, a self-cycle and a longer cycle.

analogy.familiar: Preparing workshop jobs in an order that lets each job start
analogy.connection: A prerequisite must be ready before the job that uses it.
analogy.limit: This plan orders dependencies only; it does not estimate time, people or parallel work.

steps: In `plan`, track the tasks being visited, the finished tasks, and the result list.
In `visit`, reject a task if its name is missing.
Reject a task if it is already being visited: that means there is a cycle.
Visit each task’s prerequisites in alphabetical order.
Mark the task finished after its prerequisites are finished.
Add the finished task to the result only once.
Visit the main task names in alphabetical order too.
Return `None` if a task cannot be planned; otherwise, return the result list.

checks.label: Shared prerequisites appear once in reproducible order
Cycles and missing prerequisites are reported
checks.expression: plan({"a": ["b"], "b": ["a"]}) is None and plan({"a": ["a"]}) is None and plan({"a": ["missing"]}) is None

checks.label: Empty and independent tasks work without changing input

quiz.question: You reach a task that is already in the `visiting` set. What does this tell you?
choices: It is safely finished
The current unfinished chain contains a cycle
The task has no prerequisites
quiz.explanation: Visiting holds the current unfinished chain. Returning to one of those tasks creates a circular dependency.

hints: Check visiting before treating a node as finished.
Add to visiting before recursion and remove after all prerequisites succeed.
Use sorted(tasks) and sorted(tasks[name]) without sorting input lists in place.

title: A supply category directory
summary: Create a view named category_directory with one column, category. Read supplies, omit NULL and empty-string categories, and keep each remaining category once. Display the view sorted by category. Keep spaces and capitalization as stored; the supplied categories need no cleanup.
explanation: A directory should list each category once even when many supplies belong to it. A SQL table stores rows under named columns. SELECT chooses columns; FROM chooses a table. DISTINCT removes duplicate result rows. This lesson builds a reusable directory from the supplies table rather than manually typing the category names.

SELECT DISTINCT category returns each different category value once. DISTINCT applies to the whole selected row. If you also select item_name, two rows with the same category and different items remain different rows. Choose only the column that defines the directory entry.

This self-contained example uses a temporary set of values.
```sql
WITH supplies(category) AS (
  VALUES ('paper'), ('tools'), ('paper')
)
SELECT DISTINCT category
FROM supplies
ORDER BY category;
```
The result has paper and tools once each. WITH gives this query a named input; it does not create a permanent table.

NULL represents missing information. It differs from the empty string, which is present text of length zero. Use category IS NOT NULL to omit missing values and category <> '' to omit empty text. The AND keyword requires both conditions to hold. Neither condition trims spaces or changes spelling.

A filter can run before duplicate removal.
```sql
WITH labels(name) AS (VALUES ('A'), (NULL), (''), ('A'), ('B'))
SELECT DISTINCT name
FROM labels
WHERE name IS NOT NULL AND name <> ''
ORDER BY name;
```
The result is A and B. ORDER BY requests output order explicitly; SQL does not promise a useful row order when it is omitted.

A view is a saved query, not a separate copy of its results. CREATE VIEW category_directory AS followed by SELECT defines the reusable query. Later, SELECT * FROM category_directory ORDER BY category displays it. If a new category is added to supplies, the view reads the new data without rebuilding a manual list.

The setup file creates supplies for each run. Your query should create the view without changing those source rows, then display the sorted directory. Checks look for duplicates and omitted empty values in the supplied data. After passing, add a new category in setup.sql and rerun: a real view derives its results from the source instead of storing a manually typed list.

analogy.familiar: A directory with one heading for each kind of supply
analogy.connection: DISTINCT keeps each category heading once.
analogy.limit: Distinctness follows database comparison rules; it does not know that differently spelled names might mean the same thing.

Create `category_directory` with `SELECT DISTINCT category` so each category appears once.
Leave out `NULL` and empty text.
Display the view with `ORDER BY category`.
Run the checks.

checks.label: Empty and missing categories are absent

quiz.explanation: Only category is selected, so both result rows would be Tools. DISTINCT removes that duplicate; selecting the item name too would keep the rows different.

title: A reachable contact list
summary: Create a view contact_choices with id, name and contact for every row in contacts. Prefer a nonempty trimmed email, then a nonempty trimmed phone, otherwise use "No contact yet". The stored values can be NULL, empty, or contain outside spaces. Do not change the source table.
explanation: A contact record may be missing an email, a phone number or both. NULL means a missing or unknown value in SQL. An empty string and spaces-only text are present strings, so they need cleanup before a fallback can treat them as missing. This project makes one useful display value per person.

TRIM(text) removes outside spaces in SQLite. It preserves spaces inside a phone number. TRIM(NULL) remains NULL. NULLIF(value, '') returns NULL when value is an empty string and otherwise returns value. Combining them turns an empty or spaces-only field into NULL.

This example shows the cleanup step.
```sql
WITH data(email) AS (VALUES ('  a@example.org  '), (''), ('   '), (NULL))
SELECT NULLIF(TRIM(email), '') AS cleaned
FROM data;
```
The first result is a@example.org. The remaining values are NULL. AS cleaned gives the output column a useful name.

COALESCE chooses the first argument that is not NULL. Its argument order expresses your preference: cleaned email first, cleaned phone second, a written fallback last. COALESCE does not consider a plain empty string missing; that is why the NULLIF cleanup matters.

Here is a complete fallback example.
```sql
WITH people(email, phone) AS (VALUES ('   ', ' 555 0100 '))
SELECT COALESCE(
  NULLIF(TRIM(email), ''),
  NULLIF(TRIM(phone), ''),
  'No contact yet'
) AS contact
FROM people;
```
It returns 555 0100. The outside spaces disappear but the internal space remains.

This is a display choice, not proof that an email or phone number is valid or reachable. Do not invent stricter validation than the task requests. Keep id and name in the view so a caller can associate the chosen contact with the right person. Every input person should produce one output row.

Create the contact_choices view and display it ordered by id. Check a person with both fields, phone only, neither field and spaces-only email. The preference rule must keep email when both are available. The source table should remain unchanged because formatting a view need not edit saved contact details.

analogy.familiar: Choosing the first usable contact line on a form
analogy.connection: The ordered fallbacks try email, then phone, then a clear missing-contact message.
analogy.limit: A nonempty value can still be mistyped; choosing it does not verify that it works.

steps: Use `TRIM` to remove spaces at the edges of each contact field.
Use `NULLIF` to treat empty text as missing.
Use `COALESCE` to choose email first, then phone, then the fallback message.
Make a view with `id`, `name`, and `contact` for every person.
Display the rows in `id` order.
Run the check that confirms the source data stayed unchanged.

title: An order status dashboard
summary: Create a view customer_orders with customer_id, name, total_orders, paid_orders and paid_cents. Include every customer, even those without orders. Count all their orders, count only status="paid" orders, and sum only paid amounts. Missing totals must be zero. Amounts are nonnegative integer cents.
explanation: A dashboard may need several summaries from the same data. Aggregation combines rows, using functions such as COUNT and SUM. Conditional aggregation adds a decision inside the aggregate so different summary columns can include different rows. Here, a customer can have paid, pending or cancelled orders.

Start from customers and LEFT JOIN orders using the customer ID. A left join keeps a customer even when no order matches. The unmatched order columns become NULL. COUNT(*) would count that retained row as one, so use COUNT(o.id) to count only real orders; COUNT(column) skips NULL.

CASE turns a condition into a value before SUM adds it.
```sql
WITH orders(status, cents) AS (VALUES ('paid', 300), ('pending', 500), ('paid', 200))
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM orders;
```
This returns 2 paid orders and 500 paid cents. The pending amount is deliberately excluded.

GROUP BY chooses which rows belong to each summary. Group by customer ID and name. Names alone are unsafe because two different customers can share a name. Aliases such as c for customers and o for orders shorten qualified column names, including c.id and o.customer_id.

This example keeps a customer with no order.
```sql
WITH customers(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2)),
orders(id, customer_id) AS (VALUES (10, 1))
SELECT c.id, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
ORDER BY c.id;
```
Customer 1 has one order; customer 2 has zero. An inner join would lose customer 2 entirely.

Do not place WHERE o.status = 'paid' after the join: it would remove unpaid orders before total_orders is counted and remove customers without paid orders. Put that condition inside each paid aggregate. CASE with ELSE 0 gives the retained no-order row a zero contribution.

Integer cents avoid floating-point rounding for this small monetary total. The view summarizes orders; it does not charge anyone or infer payment from an amount. Checks include two customers sharing a name, a customer with no orders and unpaid orders that must not count toward revenue. Display the final view ordered by customer_id.

analogy.familiar: One summary line for each customer on a shop report
analogy.connection: Conditional totals count different kinds of orders without losing the customer.
analogy.limit: A summary depends on the stored status; it does not verify that a real payment occurred.

steps: Use `LEFT JOIN` to match customers to orders by customer ID.
Count `o.id` to count the orders.
Use one `CASE` expression to count paid orders.
Use another `CASE` expression to add paid amounts.
Group the results by customer ID and name.
Display the view.
solution:
CREATE VIEW customer_orders AS
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS total_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS paid_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN o.amount_cents ELSE 0 END) AS paid_cents
FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
SELECT * FROM customer_orders ORDER BY customer_id;

checks.label: All orders count, but only paid amounts contribute
checks.expression: SELECT count(*)=1 FROM customer_orders WHERE customer_id=1 AND name='Alex' AND total_orders=3 AND paid_orders=2 AND paid_cents=1750

checks.label: A customer with no orders stays with zero totals
checks.expression: SELECT count(*)=1 FROM customer_orders WHERE customer_id=2 AND total_orders=0 AND paid_orders=0 AND paid_cents=0

checks.label: Matching names remain separate and unpaid orders stay unpaid
checks.expression: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM customer_orders)=3 AND (SELECT count(*) FROM customer_orders WHERE customer_id=3 AND name='Alex' AND total_orders=2 AND paid_orders=0 AND paid_cents=0)=1

choices: NULL
quiz.explanation: COUNT(o.id) counts non-NULL IDs, so there are zero orders. COUNT(*) would instead count the retained placeholder row.

Use SUM(CASE WHEN o.status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
For paid_cents, use o.amount_cents instead of 1; do not filter the whole query to paid rows.

title: A folder path explorer
summary: Create a view folder_paths with id, path and depth from folders(id, name, parent_id). Roots have NULL parent_id, path equal to their name and depth 0. Children append "/" plus their name and increase depth by 1. Include every folder in the supplied acyclic forest. Names contain no slash; keep the source unchanged.
explanation: A folder tree stores one row per folder and the ID of its parent. A root has no parent. A forest is a collection of separate trees, so there can be several roots. A recursive query repeatedly uses earlier results to find the next level. It can build full paths even when the depth varies.

A common table expression, or CTE, gives a query a temporary name after WITH. WITH RECURSIVE allows a CTE to refer to itself. It has an anchor query that provides starting rows and a recursive query that expands from them. UNION ALL combines the starting and later rows without removing duplicates.

This complete recursive example counts upward.
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
  SELECT 0
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 3
)
SELECT n FROM numbers ORDER BY n;
```
It produces 0, 1, 2 and 3. The WHERE condition prevents further expansion after 3. A recursive query needs a reason to stop.

For folder paths, the anchor selects rows whose parent_id IS NULL. Give each root its own name as the path and zero as the depth. The recursive part joins a child folder to an already discovered parent path using child.parent_id = parent.id. When no undiscovered descendants remain to expand, the supplied acyclic tree is finished.

SQLite joins text with ||. Here is a small one-level example.
```sql
WITH parent(id, path, depth) AS (VALUES (1, 'Home', 0)),
child(id, name, parent_id) AS (VALUES (2, 'Notes', 1))
SELECT child.id, parent.path || '/' || child.name AS path, parent.depth + 1 AS depth
FROM child JOIN parent ON child.parent_id = parent.id;
```
The output is ID 2, Home/Notes and depth 1. The full recursive query repeats that same expansion at every level.

The input contract guarantees an acyclic forest and existing parents. General untrusted graphs need cycle detection or another explicit bound; this exercise does not claim to handle arbitrary cycles. Start from every root so a second tree is not lost. Repeated folder names under different parents are allowed because IDs, not names, connect the rows.

Wrap the CTE query in CREATE VIEW folder_paths AS and select id, path and depth from its result. Display the view ORDER BY path. Checks include two roots, a deeper descendant and repeated names in different branches. A fixed number of self-joins would solve only a fixed depth; recursion expresses the repeated operation directly.

analogy.familiar: Following branches from each top-level folder
analogy.connection: Each discovered parent provides the starting path for its children.
analogy.limit: The supplied data is a tree; arbitrary cyclic relationships need additional handling.

Start with the root folders at depth zero.
Match each child folder to a parent already found.
Add the child’s name to the path.
Add one to the depth for each level.
Make this result available as `folder_paths`.
Display the paths in order.

Only Home, because it appears first

title: A countdown that knows when to stop
summary: Complete countdown(start). For a nonnegative integer start, return a list counting down to 1. Starting at 0 returns an empty list. Do not include 0 or change the input contract.
explanation: A while loop repeats its body while a condition is true.
Python checks the condition before each repetition. If it is false at the beginning, the body runs zero times.

Here the number changes after each display.
```python
energy = 3
while energy > 0:
    print(energy)
    energy = energy - 1
```
The displayed values are 3, 2, and 1. After energy becomes 0, the condition 0 > 0 is false.
Indentation puts both instructions inside the repeated body. If the update were outside it, energy would stay 3 and this loop would not stop.
The condition decides whether a boundary is included. With energy >= 0, the same loop would also display 0 before stopping.

You can keep repeated results in a list instead of displaying them.
```python
steps = []
remaining = 2
while remaining > 0:
    steps.append(remaining)
    remaining = remaining - 1
print(steps)
```
This produces [2, 1]. append stores the current number before the update changes remaining.
In your function, create a fresh list for each call. Return it after the loop finishes, not during the first repetition.
Try a start of 0, then 1, then 4. These distinguish an empty loop, a single repetition, and several repetitions.

analogy.familiar: Follow a small change from its starting state to its result.
analogy.connection: Each instruction changes what the next instruction receives.
analogy.limit: Use the actual code and checks rather than relying on the comparison.

    values = []
    # TODO: collect start down to 1, then return values.

solution:
def countdown(start):
    values = []
    remaining = start
    while remaining > 0:
        values.append(remaining)
        remaining = remaining - 1
    return values

print(countdown(4))

title: Keep subjects that meet the total
summary: Create a view named qualifying_subjects with subject and total_minutes. Include subjects whose summed known minutes are at least 30. Display the result ordered by subject. Do not modify sessions.
explanation: WHERE filters individual rows before they are grouped.
GROUP BY puts rows with the same group value together. SUM then adds the known numbers in each group.
HAVING filters the grouped results. It can ask a question about SUM(minutes).

This separate example keeps a group whose total reaches 20.
```sql
WITH practice(subject, minutes) AS (
  VALUES ('Drawing', 8), ('Drawing', 14), ('Singing', 15)
)
SELECT subject, SUM(minutes) AS total_minutes
FROM practice
GROUP BY subject
HAVING SUM(minutes) >= 20
ORDER BY subject;
```
Drawing remains with 22 minutes. Neither individual Drawing row reaches 20, but the total does.
Using WHERE minutes >= 20 instead would remove both Drawing rows before addition. It answers a different question.
The >= comparison includes the exact boundary. A total of 30 qualifies when the minimum is 30.
SUM ignores NULL inputs. A group with only NULL minutes has an unknown total, so it does not pass this numeric condition.
Create the view from a grouped SELECT. A view saves the query; it is not a separate copied table.

title: Try a change without moving the main branch
summary: Complete branchCode(branches, current). Return the code saved for the selected branch, or null when that branch is missing. Do not change the branch map. This is a browser model; use the supplied disposable-folder walkthrough for actual Git practice.
explanation: A Git branch is a name that points to a commit. Creating a branch does not copy your project into a second folder.
When you switch branches, Git makes that branch current. Make sure existing changes are saved safely before switching.
A commit made on a feature branch advances that branch. It does not move main automatically.

Create greeting.txt containing the single line Hello in a new disposable practice folder first. With Git configured there, create a starting commit:
```bash
git init -b main
git add greeting.txt
git commit -m "Add first greeting"
```
Run these commands only in that new practice folder, never in an unrelated repository.

Create and switch to a feature branch.
```bash
git switch -c friendly-greeting
```

Change the file to Hello, explorer and save it. Commit on the current branch.
```bash
git add greeting.txt
git commit -m "Make the greeting friendlier"
```

Switch back to main and inspect greeting.txt. It still contains Hello because main has not moved.
```bash
git switch main
git status
```

Merge the feature branch into the current main branch.
```bash
git merge friendly-greeting
git log --oneline --all --graph
```
In this simple history, main moves forward to the feature commit. The file now contains Hello, explorer.
If both branches edit the same lines differently, Git may ask you to resolve a conflict. Review both intentions, edit the file into the wanted result, test it, then stage and commit the resolution.
This displays Hi then Hello. Reading one saved entry does not replace the other.
Passing this JavaScript check does not prove you created Git branches. Confirm the real walkthrough separately by inspecting the file before and after the merge.

```python

title: Create small task records safely
summary: Define a dataclass Task with title: str and tags: list. Creating Task("Read") should give a new empty tags list for that instance. Two tasks must not share the same tags list.
explanation: A dataclass can generate routine record methods, including initialization, from declared fields.
A field annotation describes an intended type. Ordinary Python does not automatically enforce it at runtime.

This small record generates its initializer.
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

point = Point(2, 3)
print(point.x)
```
The @dataclass line applies a decorator supplied by the standard library. You use it here without implementing a decorator yourself.
A mutable default needs a new value for each instance. field(default_factory=list) calls list to create a fresh list when no value is supplied.

This separate example gives each box its own items.
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
@dataclass
class Box:
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)
```

Here are actual instance calls that reveal the factory effect. field takes the default_factory keyword and returns field configuration for dataclass, not an already-created list. The dataclass calls that factory separately when constructing each Box without an items argument.
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Box:
    items: list = field(default_factory=list)

first = Box()
second = Box()
first.items.append("Map")
print(first.items)
print(second.items)
```
It prints ['Map'] then []. append receives one item and adds it to the first list in place; the second list remains empty.
Pass list itself as the factory, not list(). The factory must be callable so a new value can be made for each instance.
Changing the first task’s tags should not change a second task. Test that behavior rather than only checking the displayed class name.
Type annotations are useful descriptions for tools, but validating outside data still requires explicit checks.

title: Find customers who have paid orders
summary: Create a view paid_customers(id,name) containing each customer with at least one paid order. Multiple paid orders must not duplicate that customer. Keep source tables unchanged.
explanation:
EXISTS asks whether a subquery returns at least one row.

The supplied practice database contains customers(id, name) and orders(id, customer_id, status). The names inside parentheses are the available columns; use these exact identifiers when reading the fixture tables.
It is a yes-or-no condition. It does not add all matching child rows to the outer result.

A correlated subquery refers to the current outer row. Run this complete example in a fresh database.
```sql
CREATE TABLE authors(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE books(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,author_id INTEGER);
INSERT INTO authors VALUES(1),(2);
INSERT INTO books VALUES(10,1),(11,1);
SELECT a.id
FROM authors AS a
WHERE EXISTS(
SELECT 1
FROM books AS b
WHERE b.author_id=a.id)
ORDER BY a.id;
SELECT a.id
FROM authors AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS(
SELECT 1
FROM books AS b
WHERE b.author_id=a.id)
ORDER BY a.id;
```
The first result contains ID 1 once, despite two matching books. The NOT EXISTS result contains ID 2.

A customer with no paid orders is excluded even if they have pending orders. A customer with several paid orders appears only once.
NOT EXISTS would ask the opposite question: no matching row. It differs from assuming every customer without a match has a zero-valued order.

title: How flex items share space
summary: Let two items start from a 120px basis, grow equally into spare space, and shrink equally when the row is narrower.
explanation: Flex container rules arrange a row; flex item rules decide how each child uses its share of space.
flex-basis gives an item’s starting size along the main axis before free space is distributed.

flex-grow controls how positive free space is shared. Equal grow factors share that free space equally; they do not always imply equal final widths when starting sizes differ.

A flex-grow factor of zero opts that item out of receiving positive extra free space. Positive grow factors determine how the growing items share that space; a zero factor does not mean the item has zero size.
flex-shrink controls shrinking when space is short. Shrink distribution also depends on the starting basis size.

With equal starting bases and equal factors, these simple items stay equal.
```css
.item { flex: 1 1 80px; min-width: 0; }
```
The shorthand order is grow, shrink, basis.
min-width: 0 allows the items to shrink below their usual minimum-content width. In real layouts, still protect readable content from clipping.
The practice has no gaps, padding or borders, so its equal widths isolate item sizing rather than extra box space.
